book_title: How a Woman Becomes a Lake
email_body:
Dear Marjorie,

In How a Woman Becomes a Lake, it is Vera's absence, rather than her presence, that sets everything moving in Whale Bay, and I was struck by how a single disappearance ripples through so many lives. Coming after Y and your O. Henry Award story "Counterblast", it feels like a book built around what goes unseen.

I would love to ask how you decided whose eyes we follow through those reverberations.

subject_line: The sleeping town of Santa Lora
email_body:
Dear Karen,

The Dreamers begins so quietly: a first-year student comes back to her dorm room, falls asleep, and simply doesn't wake up. From there the sickness spreads through Santa Lora, and the fictional Southern California town becomes a place where people sleep for days, weeks or months.

I would love to ask what draws you to the possibility of the impossible, and how you keep such a premise grounded in ordinary lives.

book_title: Eyes Bottle Dark with a Mouthful of Flowers
email_body:
Dear Jake,

Eyes Bottle Dark with a Mouthful of Flowers stays with Gallup, the place nicknamed Drunktown, and refuses to let it be only violence. The poems hold beauty and brutality side by side and are rooted in Navajo history and thought, so the book reads as a reclamation rather than a lament.

I would love to ask how growing up near Vanderwagen shaped the way you chose to map that landscape in language.

email_body:
Dear Andrew,

Heavy Metal, your Autumn House Fiction Prize novel, follows fifteen-year-old Danny in a Midwestern town as he carries the memory of finding his mother after her death. I was interested to learn it began as a short story of the same name in Jabberwock Review.

I would love to ask what changed when that story opened out into a novel, and how your years as a newspaper reporter feed into your fiction.
